reference.source: Oral medicine and dermatology reference texts
clinicalPearls: Inflammation, fissuring and crusting at one or both angles of the mouth, often sore or burning
It is typically multifactorial, combining mechanical, microbial and nutritional influences
Chronic accumulation of saliva at the commissures macerates the skin, promoting overgrowth of Candida and Staphylococcus aureus
Reduced facial height from tooth loss or ill-fitting dentures deepens the folds and predisposes to it
Nutritional deficiencies (iron, B vitamins, zinc) and immunosuppression are recognised contributors
Treatment addresses the underlying cause alongside topical antifungal or antibacterial and barrier preparations
reference.pathophysiology: Angular cheilitis develops where a persistently moist, occluded skin fold at the corner of the mouth becomes macerated and inflamed. Saliva pooling in deepened commissural folds, often due to reduced vertical facial height or drooling, creates conditions favouring colonisation by Candida species and Staphylococcus aureus, which perpetuate the inflammation. Systemic factors such as iron, vitamin B or zinc deficiency and immunosuppression impair mucocutaneous integrity and predispose to the condition, so it is best understood as a multifactorial reactive process rather than a single infection.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex or impetigo of the lip
Contact or irritant dermatitis of the perioral skin
Orofacial granulomatosis or Crohn disease involvement
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic commissural involvement
Assessment of dentition, dentures and vertical facial height
Microbiological swab where infection needs targeting
Screening for nutritional deficiencies and diabetes where recurrent
Consideration of underlying immunosuppression or systemic disease
redFlags: Persistent or recurrent disease despite treatment suggesting systemic cause
Features of underlying immunosuppression or diabetes
Extension beyond the commissures or induration
reference.prognosis: The condition responds well once contributory factors are corrected, though it recurs if the underlying cause (denture problems, deficiency, dry environment) is not addressed.
pitfalls: Treating only the surface infection without correcting mechanical or nutritional causes
Overlooking iron or vitamin deficiency in recurrent cases
Confusing it with herpes labialis or impetigo
